study.title: Exodus 6: God reaffirms his covenant, responds to unbelief and prepares the mission of Moses
study.overview: Exodus 6 shows the LORD responding to the crisis caused by Pharaoh's hardness and the discouragement of Israel. God not only promises deliverance; he reaffirms who he is, remembers his covenant with the patriarchs and defines the goal of redemption: to make Israel his people and be their God. Despite this, the people do not listen to Moses because of anguish and bondage. The chapter then resumes the mission before Pharaoh and, at an end, inserts a genealogy that confirms the legitimacy of Moses and Aaron as representatives of Israel.

outline.title: God renews his promises and reveals his name
outline.explanation: The LORD responds to Moses' affliction with the promise of decisive intervention against Pharaoh. He recalls his identity, his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the listening of the cry of Israel and the purpose of deliverance: to take them out of Egypt, to take them for his people, and to lead them to the promised land.

outline.title: The message finds resistance and the mission is reaffirmed
outline.explanation: Moses communicates the words of God, but the people do not hear him because of the weight of slavery. Then the LORD again orders Moses to speak to Pharaoh, while Moses argues that if Israel does not listen to him, Pharaoh will hear him less. Even so, God reaffirms the commandment to Moses and Aaron.

outline.title: Genealogy of Reuben, Simeon and Levi: focus on Moses and Aaron
outline.explanation: The genealogical list highlights the tribes of Reuben, Simeon and above all Levi, culminating in Amram, Moses, Aaron, and his descendants. The goal is to show the Israeli origin of the two leaders and place them within the levtic and priestly lineage.

outline.title: Identification of Moses and Aaron and the persistence of Moses" limitation
outline.explanation: The text insists that this is Moses and the Aaron to whom the LORD commanded to take Israel out of Egypt. However, Moses again presents himself as an inappropriate speecher, asking how Pharaoh will hear him. The chapter ends with this tension between the divine order and the perceived weakness of the messenger.

study.context: The chapter itself offers the immediate context: Israel is in bondage in Egypt, Pharaoh resists the commandment of God and Moses was sent to confront him. References to the covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob show that the present deliverance is linked to God's ancient promises to the patriarchs. Genealogy uses names and lineages to situate Moses and Aaron in the people they must conduct.
study.theology: This chapter insists on three central truths. First, God acts in history as the Lord faithful to his word: what he promised to the patriarchs, he fulfills in due time. Second, redemption is not only out of oppression; it is a covenant relationship: "You will be my people," and I will be your God." Third, God does not depend on human eloquence or strength to fulfill his will; Moses' weakness contrasts with the authority of the divine word. The repetition of the divine name reinforces that the center of the narrative is who God is, and not the capacity of his servants. The hardness of Pharaoh's heart and the insensitivity of the people show that deliverance requires sovereign action from God, not mere human persuasion.

scholarViews.insight: The greatest need of Israel was not only to be freed from slavery, but to know the LORD; the climax of the renewed promise is to know that he is their God.
When Moses was out of way, God reassured him promising that he would now see what the LORD would do to Pharaoh; the crisis becomes an opportunity for divine intervention.
The expression on "strong" point to the sovereign power of God, which will be shown in order to force Pharaoh to drive Israel out of the land.

questions: What does it mean, in practice, that Israel's liberation had as its main target the relationship with God and not just the change of circumstances?
Why does not the people listen to Moses even after hearing words of promise, and what does this reveal about suffering and faith?
How does Moses' declared weakness help to understand how God uses limited human instruments to fulfill his will?
study.practice: This chapter invites the reader to trust in the character of God when circumstances seem to contradict his promises. Instead of measuring divine fidelity by immediate relief, it must be remembered that God remains faithful to his covenant and acts at the right time. He also calls to humble obedience: how Moses, the servant of God may feel incapable, but the task does not depend on self-confidence, but on the word of the LORD. In the Christian life, this translates to persevere in prayer, proclaim truth even when there is little receptivity and seek more knowledge of God than just quick solutions.
study.uncertainty: The biblical text provided includes the numbering up to 30, but the notes of the commentators mainly cover verses 1-28 and, in one case, there is cross-reference to 6:20-25 without exhaustive commentary of each name. It is not possible to affirm historical details beyond what the chapter itself and the notes explain. Adam Clarke's observation of the division of the chapter in relation to verse 28 is interpretative and should not be treated as an absolute textual fact.
